When you think of the company that Steve Jobs founded some 50 years ago , your mind likely first arrives at the various devices that have truly revolutionized the way we live in the modern world, of which the company now says there are 2.5 billion in active use globally. However, Apple’s Services division — often the source of those just-small-enough-to-dismiss transactions that leave your account each month, with various cloud and content subscription payments tacked on to give users the full run of Apple’s walled garden — has become a huge part of the pie, with revenues reaching yet another record in the company’s fourth quarter. In Q4, sales from Services reached a whopping $31.57 billion, up some 9.8% from the same period last year. While that might have snapped a double-digit growth streak that had run for 12 quarters in a row, as analysts quoted by Variety observed, it still means that Apple offerings such as TV+, Music, Pay, Podcasts, News+, and others are raking in more than $13 billion more each quarter than they were five years ago. The difference between how much profit Services takes in compared to Apple’s main cash cow, the Products segment, also speaks for itself: The cost of sales on the whopping $82.9 billion that Products brought in for Q4 was $52.1 billion, while the Services segment's cost of sales for the same period was just $7.6 billion. While slowing growth and the unending popularity of Apple’s devices — the company this week said it’s unsure whether it will be able to get more iPhone Duos in by the all-important Christmas trading period, after the $2,000 foldables sold out in a matter of weeks — might mean Services will never catch up to Products in the amount of cash they generate for the company, the profit race between the two has been getting more interesting. title: 🗳️ Trading the midterms
body_text: If you’ve ever eaten a potato but wished you’d roasted a chicken, well, do American food scientists have just the foodstuff for you. It took food scientists at Cornell University more than a decade, but the Poulette – a potato that tastes like chicken – has arrived, Food and Wine Magazine reports . The quest to develop this specific new tuber began with chef Dan Barber’s love of heirloom vegetables (seriously, as someone who once sat through about a dozen courses of different kinds of obscure squash at Blue Hill at Stone Barns, I can say the guy is obsessed with the stuff), and in this case a specific type of French potato that was then crossed with a more modern varietal by researchers. The Poulette is sold by Barber’s seed company and will be available in (of course) Whole Foods’ locations in the tri-state area. Today is Election Day in the United States, and traders will be keeping a close eye on the returns to get a sense for how the partisan makeup of Washington and, in some cases more crucially, governor mansions may change for the next two years. First things first, what is likely already priced in. As it stands, prediction markets have a 94% chance * that Democrats take control of the United States House of Representatives and a 76% chance of taking the Senate . While everyone’s model is a bit different, on balance traders have been likely positioning themselves for split control in Washington, with Democrats controlling Capitol Hill and Republicans the White House. As Sam Ro points out, “the periods before and after midterm elections are famously volatile for stocks,” Markets tend to perform well once there’s a clear indication of a result, and in general equities catch some tailwinds once the uncertainty is in the rearview. In yesterday’s EntryPoint , Luke Kawa put it succinctly: “History says that just getting the midterms out of the way will be a positive for US stocks.” However, options markets have been essentially treating the midterms as a non-event. After all, with such a high chance that the House flips, at this point a divided government in Washington can be considered highly likely regardless of the outcomes of a few massive Senate races. Now, that’s not to say there’s nothing on the line here for traders. One concern coming from some analysts on the Street is that, with the midterms in the past and the risk to his coalition realized, President Trump will lose one potential reason to not escalate the politically unpopular war with Iran. That’s more a matter of timing than the actual results, though, but if I run an airline I’m not exactly looking forward to the next couple of weeks of fuel cost price action. What will be watched very closely by anyone involved in the AI trade is the performance of a number of candidates who have been riding a wave of anti-data center enthusiasm that has cut across traditional party lines . For instance, while markets still currently price her as a 37% underdog in Texas against incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, Texas Rep. Gina Hinojosa has called for an immediate moratorium on data centers. Texas has more large projects underway than any other state , and that’s been motivating voters who oppose the projects regardless of their typical politics. A win for Hinojosa would likely have ramifications for the AI trade on Wednesday, given the Lone Star state has 27 GW of data center capacity planned; wins for adversaries of the data center development across the map would likewise constrain the ability of the hyperscalers to, well, hyper scale. Polls close at different times over the course of the evening, and states tend to count votes at different speeds from one another. Some states have speedier counts and can expect their votes to be counted super quickly — Florida, after a rather infamous 2000 election, got its house in order and is now one of these — while some states are going to take some time, like Maine, which reports by township and thus will be slow to provide results. By looking at key congressional districts in states that report quickly and close early, we’ll have some indications pretty early in the evening as to how the election is likely to play out over the course of the night. It’s not perfect — the voters in Michigan and the voters in Texas will likely behave similar in general, but have enough differences that we’re not expecting a uniform swing across the map — but if you want some early insight as to how the race is going to go, here’s a few early races that election projection decision desks like DDHQ are going to be paying attention to: The first instructive polls close at 7pm, and Florida and Virginia will be the fastest to report. Look to Virginia’s 1st and 2nd District , Florida’s 15th and 25th for how the House might go. If Democrats flip VA-02, they’re on track for a good night, and if they flip VA-01 as well or hold both Florida districts the Democrats are very likely to flip the House. If Republicans flip the Florida districts, or manage to hold VA-02, they could very well hold the House. After 8, we’ll get results in Ohio and North Carolina. The bellwether districts in North Carolina are NC-01 and NC-11 , keep an eye on those for an indication of how the night will go. If there’s a call in Ohio’s Senate race for the Democrats, they’re then the favorite to flip the chamber. Just because we’ll have some strong hunches early in the evening doesn’t mean we’ll have precious clarity any time soon. With a close Senate race in Alaska that (a) won’t start posting results until after midnight Eastern Time and (b) will go to a ranked-choice instant runoff if no candidate clears 50%, it’s entirely possible that we don’t know control of the Senate by opening bell on Wednesday. title: 😬 AI's awkward earnings season
body_text: Hollywood has a new heartthrob, and the basketweaving community isn't impressed. In the new romantic comedy Wicker, Alexander Skarsgård plays a man made entirely of wicker who has become an unlikely internet sex symbol. But professional basket makers are up in arms because he's not actually wicker, which is made of traditional willow and appears to be braided rather than woven. One of the designers explained to The Guardian that it simply wouldn’t have looked right if made of actual wicker. “It is a similar reason to why, in film, we don’t make armour out of actual steel or use real swords,” they said. “This is a fantasy film.” Stocks dropped on Friday because… well, keep reading. ;) Last week was a rough one for the AI trade. Going into this earnings season, investors were looking for signs that Big Tech would either bring AI costs down or prove that its AI products are generating enough revenue to justify the price tag. For the most part, they’re still waiting. Here is a rundown of the updates we got from Big Tech this earnings season: Meta will spend more than expected but its core business is still strong. The company, which was the first of its peers to report earnings, told investors it would spend even more aggressively on AI and created a new class of nonvoting stock that could ultimately be used to help pay for it. The good news: advertising revenue came in right above Wall Street estimates. Google ’s core search business showed some signs of cracking, leading to the stocks’ worst day ever. The company's AI search summaries may be cannibalizing its main advertising business as users interact with fewer traditional search ads. The company missed revenue estimates and posted negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, after doing so for the first time in its history earlier this year. The good news: its cloud business is booming and capex came in below estimates. Google’s AI overviews are also losing money for other companies that depend on traffic. Reddit , for one, said that traffic from Google fell significantly in the quarter due to the “shift to AI mode and AI overviews.” How Google will manage to fix this is a mystery, as it’s a nuanced problem that requires balancing the needs of the AI rollout with the — oh, wait, spoke too soon, as early as Friday people were reporting that they were no longer seeing AI Mode turned on by default . It’s one thing to be expensive, we suppose, but quite another to be both expensive and costing the company revenue too. Amazon ’s core e-commerce business is also slowing, while its spending accelerates. The company's quarterly revenue and earnings missed estimates, while its capex and negative free cash flow came in above expectations — a deadly combo for the stock in this environment. Microsoft ended the week relatively scot-free. The company reported soaring cloud revenue and capex below expectations, exactly the combination investors were looking for going into the week. Separately, the company said it would offer buyouts to 60,000 employees, about a quarter of its workforce, in a cost-cutting campaign. A lot of this capex spending is going toward memory chips, which has driven up the price of the critical component to personal computers. Intel ’s sales took a hit this past quarter because PC-makers, its largest customer base, are cutting production as memory costs soar. While Intel has benefited from AI demand for its data center chips, it appears the customers for its side-gig are interfering with the supply chain for its main revenue driver. Meta, Google, Microsoft and Amazon have spent a combined $1.28 trillion dollars on capex since ChatGPT was made public in Q4 2022. At first, these companies were applauded by the stock market when that metric went up, seeing it as both proof that they were staying on the cutting edge and as a promise of future demand. But as that number keeps swelling, cash-flows go negative, and AI revenue underwhelms, investors are rethinking the massive valuations they’ve given these companies in recent years. And there may not be any going back from here. With billions already sunk into AI infrastructure and competitors racing to build even more, cutting back could mean falling behind.
